title: ILLNESS APPRAISALS AND SELF-ACTUALISATION IN PARENTS OF CHILDREN WITH RUBINSTEIN–TAYBI SYNDROME: A COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS WITH EDUCATIONAL AND THERAPEUTIC PROFESSIONALS
abstract:
Parents of children with Rubinstein–Taybi syndrome (RTS) face distinctive and often persistent caregiving stressors. The ways in which they appraise the illness—and how these appraisals differ from those of teachers and therapists—may shape parental self‑actualisation and inform the design of family‑centred support.

Four groups were compared: mothers (n = 9), fathers (n = 8), teachers (n = 9), and therapists (n = 6). Illness meaning was assessed with the Disease Related Appraisals Scale (DRAS; Polish SOWCH), and parental self‑actualisation with the AS‑5‑R (Actualization of Self Scale). Because score distributions deviated from normality, Mann–Whitney U tests (caregivers vs professionals) and Kruskal–Wallis tests (four‑group comparisons) were applied, followed by Dunn–Bonferroni contrasts. Within‑parent associations were examined using Spearman correlations.

Parents reported higher Threat, Obstacle/Loss, and Harm appraisals than professionals, whereas teachers and therapists endorsed higher Profit (benefit finding) and Value. Challenge and Importance did not differ across groups. Post hoc tests indicated that mothers scored higher than therapists and fathers higher than teachers on Threat and Harm (p < .05). Among parents, Challenge was positively associated with social relatedness, creative self‑expression, and global self‑actualisation. Profit correlated positively with social relatedness, self‑regard, and global self‑actualisation. In contrast, Value showed a negative association with self‑regard. Creative self‑expression was additionally related to Threat and Importance.

Parents often construe their child’s RTS in terms of threat and loss, yet appraising the condition as a challenge or source of potential benefit aligns with richer relationships, greater creativity, and higher self‑actualisation. Professionals already tend to endorse these more adaptive appraisals. Structured parent–professional dialogue and benefit‑finding practices may support families in shifting toward growth‑promoting meanings without minimising the genuine burdens of caregiving.
